title: COVID-19 and Vitamin D Misinformation on YouTube: Content Analysis
screen_reason: Content analysis of 77 YouTube videos returned by searches for 'COVID', 'coronavirus' and 'vitamin D' in 2020. Two-coder teams classified each video as useful (all accurate information) or misleading (any inaccurate or misleading content) against the current evidence base and sun-safety guidelines: 62/77 misleading overall, 57/77 (74%) misleading about COVID-19, 60/77 (78%) misleading about vitamin D. These are quantitative shares of items in a sample judged against external ground truth, i.e. CONTENT prevalence.

Two different coding teams for the two time points; the senior scientist reviewed all videos and coding for consistency. No kappa or percent-agreement statistic reported. The abstract's wording is 'over three-quarters'. Rank-truncated first-3-pages search set, hence denom_selection=curated.

missed_or_uncertain: Extractable but not written as rows, to avoid stacking near-duplicate variants of the same 77-video corpus (all verbatim, listed here so an adjudicator can add any of them): (a) 55/77 (71%) 'contained at least some misleading information about both COVID-19 and vitamin D' - the strictest variant; (b) 15/77 (19%) 'were accurate in their statements about vitamin D and COVID-19' (the complement of row 1, so not extracted separately); (c) 45/77 (58%) 'confused correlation with causation either directly or implicitly'; (d) 37/77 (48%) 'recommended that people engage in unsafe sun (does not fit within recommendations) or UV-related behaviors'. Conditional-denominator figures NOT extracted because their denominators are self-selected sub-samples of videos that happened to discuss a topic: 46/54 (85%) of videos discussing vitamin D as COVID-19 prevention 'did directly state or imply that vitamin D can prevent or cure COVID-19'; 37/41 (90%) of videos commenting on vitamin D treating/curing COVID-19 'contained misleading information on this topic'; 8/41 (as printed, '8 (10%) of the 77 videos') useful about prevention and 4/41 (10%) useful about treatment. Account-type splits (Table 2: medical professionals 22 misleading of 34 = 65%; news 17 of 19 = 89%; 'other' 23 of 24 = 96%) are actor-type subgroups, not platform or country splits, so no rows. FLAG FOR ADJUDICATOR: the text says medical professionals 'shared over three-quarters of the misleading videos (22/62, 35%)' - 22/62 is 35%, not three-quarters; the sentence is internally contradictory (Table 2 supports 35% of misleading videos, and 65% of medical-professional videos). No exposure, reach, sharing, recall or concentration data; view counts are reported as means by accuracy (Table 3) but never as a share of views, so no EXPOSURE row is derivable.

rob.design: Cross-sectional content analysis of a rank-truncated YouTube search set. Frame: YouTube.com searched for 'COVID', 'coronavirus' and 'vitamin D' on 10 June 2020 and 7 December 2020 using an incognito Chrome window with no Google account linked and cleared cookies/cache, default relevance sort; the first 3 pages (60 videos) were captured at each time point (120 screened). Exclusions: 27 (22.5%) discussed only one of the two topics, 13 (10.8%) duplicates, 2 (1.7%) non-English, 1 (0.8%) blocked on copyright grounds, leaving 77 (64.2%) videos with 10,225,763 combined views. Not a probability sample of YouTube; deliberately mimics 'what videos [users] would be likely to see based on simple searches'. Coding: 2-coder teams per wave using an a priori codebook (Multimedia Appendix 1) coding audio and visual content together for useful vs misleading, unsafe sun exposure and correlation/causation confusion; disagreements resolved by consensus discussion with the senior author as third reviewer. No inter-rater reliability statistic reported; the authors acknowledge two different coding teams across time points as a limitation. Chi-square/Fisher exact tests for associations.
rob.item6_quote: a team of 2 coders (authors SF/EQ, SLF/CFS) used the code book to code all videos for useful (all accurate information) or misleading (any inaccurate or misleading content) COVID-19 and vitamin D information, unsafe sun exposure recommendations, and confusing correlation with causation. In particular, videos were tagged as misleading if they included information that vitamin D prevents or cures COVID-19, which is a statement that is not in line with the current evidence base, which presently only concludes a correlation between the 2 [34].
rob.item10_quote: Nearly three-quarters (57/77, 74%) of the videos contained at least some misleading information about COVID-19, and 60 (78%) contained misleading information about vitamin D (Table 1, Figure 2).
